study.title: Psalm 64 - God undoes the hidden plans of the wicked
study.overview: Psalm 64 is a prayer of deliverance before enemies who attack with hidden words, intrigues and traps. David asks for protection because the threat is real and subtle: violence comes not only through actions, but also through perverse discourses, secret planning and bitter accusations. The psalm also announces that God will reverse wickedness, causing the very sin of the wicked to fall upon them. The final result is double: fear among men before the work of God and joy, trust and praise among the righteous.

outline.title: Succin for protection
outline.explanation: David cries out to God to hear his voice and keep his life from enemy terror. He asks for concealment and preservation in the face of an organized hostility, not just an isolated conflict.

outline.title: Description of secret wickedness
outline.explanation: Enemies hurt through the tongue, as if their words were weapons. They plot in secret, trust impunity, and investigate perversities with the intention of reaching the innocent without being seen.

outline.title: Divine judgment and reaction of the righteous
outline.explanation: God answers with righteousness: he strikes the wicked, makes their tongue stumble and makes public their defeat. This judgment leads men to recognize the work of God, as the righteous rejoice, trust and glorify him.

study.context: The notes indicate that the psalm is of David and that it was composed amid the pursuit of enemies, persecutors and defamators. There is no consensus in the notes on a specific historical occasion; some readings mention persecution by Saul, others the rebellion of Absalom, and another possibility is a later context. The text, however, does not depend on setting a unique event to be understood: it depicts the recurring experience of the fair surrounded by slander, secret plan and violence.
study.theology: The psalm presents a clear theology of God's justice. First, the Lord is not indifferent to the hidden evil: he hears the prayer and sees what men do not see. Second, wickedness has a self-destructive logic; the tongue that hurts also stumbles, and the hidden plans end up exposed. Third, the judgment of God is not mere punishment, but public revelation of his righteousness, producing reverent fear in men. Finally, the proper response of the righteous is joy in the Lord, trust in him and praise, because the final security is not in human cunning, but in the faithfulness of the righteous God.

scholarViews.insight: Perverse words are described as weapons that kill; the comment also admits that this can allude to magical practices, emphasizing the destructive force of ungodly speech.

The psalm shows the continual opposition between the wickedness of the persecutors and the care of God, who protects the righteous and causes the defeat of the wicked to redouble in glory to God and encouragement for his people.
God's judgment is portrayed as a response corresponding to the plan of enemies: they try to hurt in secret, but the Lord reaches them and makes public their ruin.

questions: How can my way of speaking become a weapon, rather than serving the truth and building?
When I face hidden or unjust opposition, I first seek the protection of God or try to control everything by my own strength?
The contemplation of God's righteousness in the midst of wickedness aroused in me fear, trust and praise, as at the end of the psalm?
study.practice: Pray honestly when facing hidden attacks, defamation or injustice. Instead of answering in the same coin, handing over the cause to God, watch his words and practice transparency and righteousness. The psalm also calls the church to trust that the Lord sees what is hidden, so concrete application is to persevere without giving in to fear, without feeding revenge and without using the tongue to injure. Seeing the righteousness of God, cultivate public gratitude and encourage others to trust in him.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow the accurate historical occasion of the psalm to be safely identified. There are also, among the commentators, different possibilities about the specific scenario, and a reading mentions even a possible context after the period of David. In addition, Tyndale's reference in 64:3 to magical practices is presented as interpretive possibility, not as a certainty of the text.
